# Going Further with Excel {#sec-excel-further}

The first chapter covered how a spreadsheet works.  This one covers the functions that make
Excel worth using on real data: calculations that apply to only part of a table, pulling
values in from a second table, and summarizing a long table by category.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Calculate on part of a table with `IF`, `COUNTIF`, `SUMIF` and `AVERAGEIF`
- Build a criterion from a value you have to calculate first
- Pull a value in from a second table with `XLOOKUP`, and read the older `VLOOKUP`
  and `INDEX`/`MATCH` versions when you meet them
- Sort and filter a table without corrupting it, and know why a filter does not
  change what a formula returns
- Recognize wide and long data, and say which one a task needs
- Summarize a table by category with a PivotTable

## Conditional Functions {#sec-conditional-functions}

Everything so far has applied to a whole column.  Just as often you want an answer about
part of it -- the average yield on the canola fields, the number of fields over 60 bushels.
Excel handles this with a family of functions that take a condition alongside the range.

`COUNTIF` counts the rows that match, `SUMIF` adds them up, and `AVERAGEIF` averages them.
Each takes the range to test, the condition to test for, and (for `SUMIF` and `AVERAGEIF`)
the range holding the numbers you actually want.  `IF` is the simpler cousin: it looks at one
cell and returns one of two things.

The worksheet works through all of them on eight fields.  Column E labels each field with
`IF`, and the block underneath answers six questions about subsets.  Column F and column C
show the formulas.

::: {.workbook-callout}
::: {.excel-embed}
<iframe width="402" height="700" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" src="https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B914bfd54-1893-4ea6-a069-8c393ea9a169%7D&action=embedview&wdAllowInteractivity=False&wdDownloadButton=True&wdInConfigurator=True"></iframe>
:::

[Download this workbook](textbook_examples/mod01_conditional.xlsx) · [blank version to fill in yourself](textbook_examples/mod01_conditional_practice.xlsx) · [Open online](https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B914bfd54-1893-4ea6-a069-8c393ea9a169%7D&action=default) (File → Save a Copy to view formulas and edit)
:::

The last row of that worksheet is the one worth studying.  When the number you are comparing
against has to be calculated -- "how many fields beat the average?" -- you cannot write
`">AVERAGE(D5:D12)"`, because everything inside quotation marks is treated as literal text.
Excel would go looking for a cell containing those characters.  Instead you glue the `>` onto
the calculated number with `&`:

```
=COUNTIF(D5:D12,">"&AVERAGE(D5:D12))
```

Two more that come up constantly.  `COUNT` counts cells containing numbers; `COUNTA` counts
any cell that is not empty, text included.  And a blank cell is not a zero: `AVERAGE`,
`COUNT` and `MEDIAN` skip blanks, which is nearly always what you want.  If you fill the
blanks with zeros first, those zeros become real measurements and drag the average down.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Lookup Functions {#sec-lookup}

Data usually arrives split across tables.  You have yields by field in one place and crop
prices in another, and you need them together.  Pulling a value from the second table into
the first is a **lookup**.

`XLOOKUP` takes three things: the value to find, the column to search in, and the column to
return from.  The worksheet below has a price list off to the side in H4:I7, and column E
looks up each field\'s crop to bring back its price.

::: {.workbook-callout}
::: {.excel-embed}
<iframe width="402" height="700" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" src="https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B1dc1b36e-393e-462b-b395-b6bd1fe4eae0%7D&action=embedview&wdAllowInteractivity=False&wdDownloadButton=True&wdInConfigurator=True"></iframe>
:::

[Download this workbook](textbook_examples/mod01_lookup.xlsx) · [blank version to fill in yourself](textbook_examples/mod01_lookup_practice.xlsx) · [Open online](https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B1dc1b36e-393e-462b-b395-b6bd1fe4eae0%7D&action=default) (File → Save a Copy to view formulas and edit)
:::

Underneath, the same lookup is written three ways.  `XLOOKUP` is the one to use.  `VLOOKUP`
is older and still everywhere, so you need to be able to read it, but it has two traps: it
can only search the *first* column of its table, and its last argument defaults to
approximate matching.  Leave that argument off and Excel will happily return a wrong answer
without complaint, so always pass `FALSE`.  `INDEX`/`MATCH` was the workaround before
`XLOOKUP` existed and turns up in older workbooks.

Sometimes one column is not enough to identify a row.  If each row is one rural municipality
in one year, then RM 1 appears many times over and looking up "RM 1" finds only whichever
year happens to come first.  You need to match on RM *and* year.  The trick is to join them
into a single key with a separator:

```
=XLOOKUP(1 & "|" & 2023, B2:B10650 & "|" & A2:A10650, E2:E10650)
```

The separator earns its keep.  Without it, RM 1 in 2023 and RM 12 in 023 would both collapse
to `12023`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Sorting and Filtering {#sec-sort-filter}

**Sort** reorders the rows by one or more columns: click inside the data, then **Data →
Sort**.  The one thing to get right is the selection.  If you highlight a single column and
sort it, Excel reorders that column and leaves the rest where they are, so every row now
carries some other row\'s numbers.  Click one cell inside the table and let Excel take the
whole thing.

**Filter** hides the rows that do not match a condition: **Data → Filter**, then use the
dropdown on any column heading.  Nothing is deleted; clearing the filter brings everything
back.  It is the quickest way to look at one crop or one year in a large table.
`Ctrl+Shift+L` on Windows, `⌘⇧F` on a Mac, toggles it.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Filters hide rows from *you*, not from your formulas
This trips up almost everyone. If you filter a column to show only 2023 and then write `=AVERAGE(E2:E10650)`, Excel **still averages every row** — including the hidden ones. Ordinary functions (`AVERAGE`, `SUM`, `MEDIAN`, `STDEV.S`, `QUARTILE.INC`, …) ignore the filter completely. You would get the 1990–2025 average, not the 2023 average, and never notice.

To compute a statistic on a *subset*, do one of these:

- **Copy the visible rows to a new sheet, then compute there** (the recommended workflow for this course). After filtering, select the visible data, copy, and paste into a fresh sheet — only the visible rows come along — then run your formulas on that clean subset.
- Or use a conditional function that does the filtering itself: `AVERAGEIF`, `SUMIF`, `COUNTIF` (covered above), which never rely on hidden rows.
- Or use `SUBTOTAL` / `AGGREGATE`, which are the two functions that *do* respect filters (optional, more advanced).

Whenever a task says "for the 2023 data, compute …," your first move should be to isolate that subset — do not just filter and point a formula at the whole column.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Wide vs. Long Data {#sec-wide-long}

The same numbers can be laid out in two ways, and which one you have decides what you can
do with them.  The workbook below has the two shapes on separate tabs, with a page at the
front explaining the difference.

::: {.workbook-callout}
::: {.excel-embed}
<iframe width="402" height="700" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" src="https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B3f9ef55b-c090-4e58-bf78-03239a045680%7D&action=embedview&wdAllowInteractivity=False&wdDownloadButton=True&wdInConfigurator=True"></iframe>
:::

[Download this workbook](textbook_examples/mod01_wide_long.xlsx) · [Open online](https://usaskca1-my.sharepoint.com/personal/pjs998_usask_ca/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B3f9ef55b-c090-4e58-bf78-03239a045680%7D&action=default) (File → Save a Copy to view formulas and edit)
:::

In the **wide** table, the crop is the column heading -- three crops, three columns.  In the
**long** table, the crop is a value sitting in its own column, and every yield is stacked
into a single Yield column.  Same data, different shape.

Wide is easy to read and convenient for column-at-a-time arithmetic: average the Canola
column and you are done.  Long is what you need when you want to summarize *by* the thing
that is stacked.  A PivotTable can only group by a field that lives in its own column, so if
you want average yield by crop, the crop has to be a column of values rather than a set of
headings.

Neither is wrong.  Reshaping between them by hand in Excel is tedious, which is one of the
arguments for moving to R -- there it is a single function call in each direction
(`pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`).  You will meet the formal version of this idea,
called tidy data, in @sec-tidy-data-chapter.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Other resources — wide vs. long data

- **R for Data Science (Wickham)** — the [Data tidying chapter](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy) is the definitive treatment of tidy data and the wide/long distinction (we return to this in Module 3).
- **Video (concept + reshaping)** — Riffomonas Project, [*Reshaping data to be long or wide with pivot_longer and pivot_wider*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVddiwrbrr4). Uses R, but the *idea* of wide vs. long is exactly what we need here.
:::


## PivotTables {#sec-pivottables}

A PivotTable summarizes a long table by category -- total acres by crop, average yield by
year -- without writing any formulas.  You drag the field you want to group by into one box
and the field you want to summarized into another, and Excel builds the table.  The name
comes from being able to pivot it: put crops down the side and years across the top, then
swap them, then add a third field, all by dragging.

To build one: click a cell inside your data, then **Insert → PivotTable**, and put the result
on a new sheet.  You get an empty table and a field list.  Drag a category into **Rows**,
another into **Columns** if you want a two-way table, and the number you care about into
**Values**.  Excel sums the values by default; click on the value to change it to Average,
Count, Max or anything else.  **Filters** applies a condition to the whole table.

Then experiment.  Dragging fields in and out costs nothing and is the fastest way to find out
what the data says.

A caution before you read anything into a comparison: check that the categories share a unit.
A PivotTable will rank crops by average "yield" whether or not some are in bushels per acre
and others in pounds, and the pounds crop will look enormously better for no reason at all.

A **PivotChart** is a chart tied to a PivotTable -- **PivotTable Analyze → PivotChart**.  It
updates when the table does.

Other things worth knowing: right-click a value and **Summarize Values By** changes the
aggregation, **Show Values As** turns it into a percentage of the row, column or total, and
**Refresh** picks up changes to the underlying data.  Double-clicking any cell in the table
creates a new sheet containing the rows that produced that number, which is the quickest way
to check a figure that looks wrong.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Excel Efficiency: Tips and Tricks {#sec-excel-tricks}

Everything above is about *what* to compute. This short section is about doing it *faster*. None of it is required to get the right answer — but once your datasets are bigger than a single screen (and the real ones in this course have thousands of rows), moving around with the mouse becomes painfully slow. A handful of keyboard habits will make you dramatically quicker, and they are worth building early.

### Moving Around a Worksheet {.unnumbered}

The mouse is fine for a small sheet. But scrolling to the bottom of a 10,000-row column by dragging is misery. The keyboard jumps you there instantly. The shortcuts differ slightly between a Mac and a PC — on a Mac you generally use the **Command (⌘)** key where Windows uses **Ctrl** — so both are given below.

| Action | Mac | Windows |
|--------|-----|---------|
| Jump to the edge of a block of data (top/bottom/left/right) | `⌘` + arrow | `Ctrl` + arrow |
| Jump *and select* everything along the way | `⌘` + `Shift` + arrow | `Ctrl` + `Shift` + arrow |
| Select the whole column of data from here down | `⌘` + `Shift` + `↓` | `Ctrl` + `Shift` + `↓` |
| Go to cell `A1` (the top-left) | `⌘` + `Fn` + `←` | `Ctrl` + `Home` |
| Go to the last cell with data | `⌘` + `Fn` + `→` | `Ctrl` + `End` |
| Move one cell (any direction) | arrow keys | arrow keys |
| Move to the next cell after typing | `Enter` (down) / `Tab` (right) | `Enter` / `Tab` |
| Edit the cell you are on (without retyping) | `Ctrl` + `U` or double-click | `F2` |

The workhorse is **`⌘`/`Ctrl` + arrow**: it flies to the edge of the current block of data. Sitting at the top of a column of yields and want the bottom? `⌘`+`↓`. Add **`Shift`** and it *selects* everything on the way — so `⌘`+`Shift`+`↓` grabs the entire column of numbers, which is exactly how you feed a range into `=SUM(...)` or `=AVERAGE(...)` without dragging. (Careful: `⌘`+arrow stops at the first *blank* cell. If your column has a gap, it stops there — press again to continue past it. This is also a handy way to *find* accidental blanks in your data.)

### A Few More Time-Savers {.unnumbered}

- **The fill handle.** The small square at the bottom-right corner of a selected cell. Drag it to copy a formula down a column (references adjust as you learned in [Relative and Absolute References](module01a.qmd#sec-references)), or **double-click** it to auto-fill down as far as the neighbouring column has data — no dragging.
- **AutoSum.** Select a cell just below a column of numbers and press `Alt`+`=` (Windows) or `⌘`+`Shift`+`T` (Mac); Excel guesses the range and writes the `=SUM(...)` for you. (If the shortcut does not fire on your version, the **AutoSum** button — the Σ on the Home tab — does the same thing.)
- **Undo / Redo.** `⌘`+`Z` / `⌘`+`Shift`+`Z` (Mac), `Ctrl`+`Z` / `Ctrl`+`Y` (Windows). Undo is your safety net — experiment freely, then undo.
- **Freeze panes.** **View → Freeze Panes → Freeze Top Row** keeps your header row visible while you scroll through thousands of rows, so you never lose track of which column is which.
- **Copy a value, not the formula.** Copy a cell, then **Paste Special → Values** to paste the *result* rather than the formula — useful when you want to lock in a number so it stops recalculating.

::: {.takeaway}
You do not need any of these to get the right answer — but the keyboard is far faster than the mouse once data gets large. Learn `⌘`/`Ctrl` + arrow first; it alone will save you hours over the term.
:::
